en: Auspiciousness.
Having paid homage to the Supreme Goddess of Speech, who possesses a threefold form,
the essential meaning of the *Guru-alaṅkāra-sūtras* is here stated by means of a commentary.

INTRODUCTION: Here, indeed, the ancient authors on poetics, such as Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, and others, consider the suggested meaning (pratīyamāna-artha) to be included within the category of figures of speech (alaṅkāra) because it serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning (vācya).
This is evident in cases such as *paryāyokta*, *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, *samāsokti*, *ākṣepa*, *vyājastuti*, *upameyopamā*, *ananvaya*, and so forth.

They have explained that the mere matter (*vastumātra*), while being understood, serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning through two modes according to the circumstances— namely, "attracting another for its own establishment" and "surrendering itself for the sake of another. Rudraṭa also stated that the figure of speech *bhāva* is of two kinds.
In figures such as *rūpaka*, *dīpaka*, *apahnuti*, and *tulyayogitā*, ornaments like simile (*upamā*) are stated to function as embellishments of the expressed meaning (*vācya*).
However, poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is said to be manifested by itself.
Furthermore, in cases such as *rasavat* and *preyas*, rasa, bhāva, and so forth are stated to serve as causes for the beauty of the expressed meaning.
Thus, all three types of *pratīyamāna* (the suggested) have indeed been proclaimed as figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
However, Vāmana, by asserting that *lakṣaṇā* based on similarity constitutes the figure of speech *vakrokti*, described a certain variety of *dhvani* merely as a figure of speech;
he stated that *rīti*, consisting of the arrangement of words characterized by specific qualities (*guṇa*), is the very soul of poetry (*kāvyātmatva*).
Udbhaṭa and others, however, have indicated that there is essentially no difference between the *guṇas* and the *alaṅkāras*,
because they establish their distinction merely on the basis of their respective domains and because they both function as properties of poetic composition (*saṃghaṭanā*).

Thus, it is the view of the ancients that figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) alone are the primary element in poetry. However, the author of the *Vakroktijīvita* has declared that various forms of "crooked expression" (*vakrokti*), whose nature consists in the artful phrasing of wit (*vaidagdhya-bhaṅgī-bhaṇiti*), are the very life of poetry by virtue of their primacy;
he further maintained that the primacy belongs to the function (*vyāpāra*) of poetry.
The figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) are indeed specific modes of expression;
even though a threefold distinction is perceived, it is the verbal formulation (*bhaṇiti*), consisting of a functional operation, that constitutes the domain of the poet’s creative effort.
Through such devices as metaphorical deviation (*upacāravakratā*) and others, the entire expanse of *dhvani* is subsumed.
The established view of that [school] is that poetry has its life solely in the variety of *mukti* (liberation), and not in the life of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).

However, Bhaṭṭanāyaka, by asserting that the function of suggestion— which he accepts through bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*)— constitutes an integral part of poetry, declared the primacy of that very function over the nature of word and meaning, which it subordinates.

In that regard as well, a function consisting of the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of rasa— which transcends the two functions characterized as denotation (*abhidhā*) and manifestation (*bhāvakatva*)— is accepted as the primary locus of repose, being synonymous with "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). Furthermore, since the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* maintains that the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), which is denoted by terms such as "resounding" (*dhvanana*) or "illuminating" (*dyotana*) and which transcends the triad of functions known as denotation, intentionality (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*),
must necessarily be admitted, and because a mere function cannot constitute the meaning of a sentence, it is the sentence-meaning itself [that is the primary element].

And since that which is of the nature of the suggested (vyaṅgya) is the soul (ātman), he established this on the grounds that it possesses primacy as the object to be embellished by the qualities (guṇas) and ornaments (alaṅkāras), and because it is the locus of final repose. Since the operation (vyāpāra) acquires its own form by way of its object, it possesses primacy through the primacy of that object; thus, because it lacks the status of being investigated in its own right, the object alone is capable of bearing the entire burden. Therefore, it must be stated that the object itself, known as the "suggested," is the life-force (jīvita).
That which possesses the splendor resulting from the adoption of beauty produced by qualities (*guṇa*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*),
yet for which the *rasas* and so forth are the very lifeblood and cannot be called ornaments—
because ornaments serve only as embellishments.

Furthermore, since rasa and the other elements are primarily that which is to be embellished, it follows that the suggested meaning alone, having become the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), constitutes the life of poetry; this is the very position that wins over those sensitive critics (*sahṛdaya*) who understand the nature of sentence-meaning. For the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vyāpāra*) cannot be denied by anyone, and no alternative position can be established upon the basis of that function.

As for the author of the *Vyaktiviveka*, who asserted that suggestion (*vyañjanā*) is included within inference because the expressed meaning functions as a logical mark (*liṅga*) with respect to the suggested meaning—that was an unexamined statement, since there is no identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) between the expressed and the suggested. This matter is so profound that it must be scrutinized by those with sharp intellects; thus, it is not elaborated upon here.
Nevertheless, the function of suggestion directed toward the suggested meaning certainly exists.

In that regard, based on the predominance or non-predominance of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), there are two varieties of poetry called *dhvani* (suggestion) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion).
When the suggested meaning is not clearly manifest, there is a third variety of poetry called *citra* (pictorial).
Among these, *dhvani* is the highest.

Since that [suggestion] has as its basis both indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and denotation (*abhidhā*), it has two divisions: the one called "the expressed meaning is unintended" (*avivakṣitavācya*) and the one called "the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate" (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).

The first of these is also twofold, by virtue of being "the expressed meaning transferred to another meaning" (*arthāntarasaṃkramita*), "the expressed meaning whose sequence is imperceptible" (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), and "the expressed meaning entirely set aside" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*).
The second is also twofold, by virtue of having a suggested meaning whose sequence is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*) or whose sequence is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).

There is *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact) based on *lakṣaṇā* (indication) and rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*), which is of the type where the sequence [of suggestion] is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*). There is *rasādidhvani* (suggestion of rasa and so forth) rooted in the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*), which is of the type where the sequence is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*). And there is both *vastudhvani* and *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of a fact or a poetic figure) rooted in the power of both word and meaning (*śabdārthobhayaśaktimūla*), which is also of the type where the sequence is perceptible.
Among those, the suggestion of rasa and so forth has been demonstrated in the *Alaṅkāramañjarī*,
because erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is the predominant element of poetry;
the remainder, however, has been classified therein according to the appropriate occasion.

Subordinate suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) has been shown in its various forms— such as being subordinate to the expressed meaning (*vācya*) and so forth— as they occur in figures like *samāsokti* and others. However, *citra* (verbal and ideal ornamentation), by its very nature as consisting of word-ornaments (*śabdālaṃkāra*) and meaning-ornaments (*arthālaṃkāra*), possesses a much greater number of subdivisions.
For instance, there are three types of repetition here: repetition of meaning, repetition of words, and repetition of both word and meaning.

The statement regarding the types of tautology (*paunaruktya*) at the beginning is for the purpose of establishing the classification of the poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) that are about to be described.

Although the word is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the meaning in the process of cognition, the definition of "semblance of tautology" (*punaruktavad-ābhāsa*) is given first because of its long-standing traditional renown; the purpose here is to provide its definition prior to the others.
In this context, the word *iha* refers to the subject matter (*prasthāna*).
The word *iti* indicates a manner;
for the completion of the number is already established by the word *tri* itself.
In that regard, the repetition of meaning is a deeply rooted fault.
There is a twofold division based on whether [the realization] has taken root or not.
The first statement regarding what is to be abandoned is for the purpose of resting in that which is to be adopted.
The word "therein" (tatra) serves to specify among the three.
Settling into the manifestation as it appears is "germination.
Furthermore, appearing as if repeated again and again is "repetition" (praroha). *Sūtra 3*. *RuAss* 3.
The use of the masculine form [in the compound] at the beginning is for the purpose of understanding that there is a change [in gender] at the end.

In the definition of the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*), the neuter gender is not used in order to suggest, by contrast with worldly ornaments, that poetic ornaments (*kāvyālaṅkāra*) are dependent upon the object to be ornamented (*alaṅkārya*).
It should be understood that they are "ornaments of meaning" (*arthālaṅkāra*) precisely because they depend on the meaning, due to the repetition of meaning and so forth.
The specific divisions are not stated here for fear of prolixity;
an example may be found in my *Śrīkaṇṭhastava* as follows: "His body is encircled by the coils of the lord of serpents..."
The life-story of Nandi, beginning with Śailādi, which shattered the pride of Kandarpa.
I bow to the Lord, the companion of Pārvatī, who bears the mark of the preeminent bull, whose eyes are like fire and the sun, and who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
Born from wood, fierce, the supreme reducer of things to ashes,
with intense red and crimson flames— may the crested Fire protect you.
May Śiva— who wears serpents as earrings, whose cool rays are as bright as the manifest moon,
and who captivates the heart— always protect the worlds from calamity.
START Sūtra 4: Repetition of sound consists of repetition of phonemes alone, and repetition of the collection of vowels and consonants. // RuAss_4 //

In the discussion of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), mere repetition of sounds is not counted because it lacks beauty; thus, there are only two types. Regarding the restriction of number, *chekānuprāsa* (alliteration) comes first. [Sūtra 5]
The rule regarding number is that there is a manifold similarity between two groups of consonants [in the case of alliteration].
The first type, which relies on a group of preceding consonants, is as follows:
"O frog of wicked resolve, why indeed do you produce such a sound by squeezing your body in the evening, as if out of anger?"
Having heard these sweet, black-throated warblings of the swans in their play, are you not ashamed?

Here, by the word *sāyam*, there is a *saṃkara* (commingling) with *vṛttyanuprāsa* (alliteration), characterized by their being expressed through a single designation, based on the similarity of the mere letter *y*.
*Chekāḥ* means the clever.
START Sūtra 6:
Otherwise, however, it is *vṛttyanuprāsa*.

Similarity consisting solely of consonants is one type; similarity of the whole [word] and mutual similarity among three or more [words] are other types; "otherwise-ness" (anyathābhāva) is the transformation. *Vṛtti*, however, is the operation directed toward rasa; that which possesses this is *vṛtti* in the context of the arrangement of phonemes (*varṇa*).
And that [alliteration] is threefold, because it is composed of harsh, soft, or intermediate syllables;
this *anuprāsa* is characterized by those [syllables].
For example:
"Even though that speech of a poet may sport at the outset with great and skillful bombast, it nevertheless does not provide delight to the minds of the wise;

for there can be no such delight until there arises a *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) resonant with the humming of abundant and beautiful qualities and ornaments, following the downpour of the flowing essence of nectar."
Or as it is said:

"The flaming crests of fire spat by serpents, or even showers of iron arrows; the rays of the autumn moon that discharge liquid poison, or the winds during the rainy season—none of these are as unbearable as these glances of the deer-eyed women, straight yet sidelong, white and dark in luster, languid, full of intent, impassioned, and pierced by the shafts of pride."
START Sūtra 7: Yamaka (chiasmus) is the repetition of a combination of vowels and consonants. // RuAss_7 //

In this regard, there are briefly three types: in some cases there is a difference in meaning, in some cases an identity of meaning, and in some cases one word is meaningless while the other is meaningful.
For example:
"Whosoever beholds her beautiful eyes becomes [like] a lotus-born [Brahmā]."
In each of those other eyes, no pleasure whatsoever arises.
This is in the case of meaningfulness;
in this same way, other [cases] are to be understood.
START Sūtra 8:
“The fault that has taken root is the tautology of word and meaning.”
The inclusion of the term "established" (*praruḍha*) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the various classifications that will be explained hereafter.
As they say: "The repetition of words or meanings is tautology (*punarukta*), except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*)."
START Sūtra 9:
"But Lāṭānuprāsa consists in a difference of intended meaning. // RuAss_9 //
Tātparya is the state of being directed toward another [meaning].
Only that is differentiated, not the essential nature of the word or its meaning.
As it is said:
"The virtues of those who are perceived by their own companions become manifest;
like lotuses bathed in the rays of the sun, they blossom."
"Virtues arise only when they are perceived by those with sensitive hearts;
lotuses become truly lotuses only when graced by the rays of the sun."
"O lotus-eyed one, close your eyes for just a brief moment; we shall say how much time has passed.
O young woman, know this: having swiftly seized that golden lotus, here I am, come as the enemy of the gods."

In such instances as this, although there is no tautology regarding the case endings and so forth, because of the tautology of the meanings of many words, it is indeed *lāṭānuprāsa* (alliteration of the Lat country). For example:
"The *kāśa* reeds shine like *kāśa* reeds; the lakes are like lakes;
and the rivers, like rivers, have captivated the hearts of the youths."
In such cases, there is no *saṃkara* (commixture) between this [figure] and *ananvaya*, characterized by their being expressed by a single statement;
for they are established as having distinct domains, since one resides in both word and meaning while the other resides in meaning alone, with respect to their mutual dependence.
And in *ananvaya*, the identity of the word is incidental, arising from propriety.
In this case of alliteration (*lāṭānuprāsa*), however, the motive is indeed direct.
Thus, in this manner, there are five ornaments regarding repetition. // RuAss_10 //
This has been explained by the [preceding] statement.
Sūtra 11:
It is a marvel that phonemes should be the cause of forms such as swords and the like! RuAss 11.

In the context of tautology (*paunaruktakya*), "variegated speech" (*citram vacanam*) consists of the repetition of syllables associated with specific positions [in a composition]. Although written characters (*lipyakṣara*) are distinguished by their particular arrangements such as the sword-form (*khaḍga*) and so forth, they are nonetheless perceived in common worldly usage as non-different from the sounds (*śabda*) consisting of syllables inherent in the auditory faculty and space; therefore, this is an ornament of expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*).
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), compositions such as the lotus-form (*padmabandha*) are also included, as far as their formation is possible according to linguistic convention.

"Just as it appears: 'O assembly, alas! It shines with the splendor of the gods, yet its divisions are destroyed; it is devoid of the manifestation of aesthetic flavor, though its essence is cultivated through the perception of impurity.'"
This is the eight-petaled lotus seat.
Here, in the petals of the cardinal directions, there is a joining of syllables through both exit and entry;
however, in the intermediate petals, it is otherwise.
The syllable *karṇikā*, however, is indeed [the word] *śliṣṭa*.
Sūtra 12:
Metaphor (*upamā*) consists in the similarity between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, wherein there is an equality of difference and non-difference.

This is the section on figures of sense (*arthālaṅkāra*). The phrase "of the object of comparison and the subject of comparison" is intended to exclude cases where the object of comparison or the subject of comparison is not well-known. Regarding similarity (*sādharmya*), there are three types.
The predominance of difference is like *vyatireka* and so forth;
the predominance of non-difference is like *rūpaka* and so forth;
the equality of both is as in this [present case].
As they say: "Where there is some commonality and some distinction, that is the object of similarity.
Simile itself, through its manifold varieties of diversity, serves as the seed for numerous other figures of speech; thus, it is mentioned first.
Regarding this, the ancients have described its many types based on the distinctions between the complete (*pūrṇā*) and the elliptical (*luptā*).

In that regard as well, a common attribute (sādhāraṇadharma) is sometimes described with a single form due to its pervasive intensity, and sometimes it is described separately through the relation of object-to-counterpart (vastu-pratibastubhāva).
And in the case of separate description, there is merely a difference in the related entities, as in the case of *prativastūpamā*.
Or, it is like the relationship between an object and its reflection,
as in the following examples in sequence:
"Like a lamp with its flame pointing upward, like the threefold path of the one who possesses the three paths."
By that very speech, which possesses refinement, the wise man is both purified and adorned.
"As she departed, repeatedly turning her neck and bearing that face which resembled a lotus with its stalk twisted back—
the side-glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman, smeared as it were with both nectar and poison, has been driven deep into my heart."

In this case, "curvature" (*valutatva*) and "roundness" (*āvṛttatva*) are distinct due to the difference in their correlates; however, from the perspective of the substratum (*dharmī*), they constitute nothing other than the relationship of the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbatva*).
"This Pāṇḍya king has a long necklace resting upon his shoulders, his body is anointed with yellow sandalwood paste..."
It shines like the king of mountains, its peaks reddened by the morning sun and emitting a cascade of waterfalls.
In this instance, the necklace and the redness [of the lips] are indicated as reflections of a waterfall and the morning sunlight, respectively.
START Sūtra 13:
When one and the same thing serves as both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, it is *ananvaya* (non-correspondence). // RuAss_13 //
The conformity with the preceding form is intended according to the literal meaning (*vācyābhiprāyeṇa*).
However, the connection of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmasaṃsarga*) in one [subject] is for the purpose of excluding a second companion (*savrahyacārin*).
For this very reason, the application (*yoga*) of the term "non-concomitance" (*ananvaya*) is also possible here.
"Just as Arjuna, whose prowess was renowned like that of the god Arjuna, and Bhima, whose deeds were terrifying toward his enemies like the god Bhima,
both proceeded with great care to the lord of Nyagrodhavatī in order to terrify the Kurus."
START Sūtra 14: When two things are compared to each other by turns, that is Upameyopamā (the comparison of the object of comparison with the standard of comparison). RuAss_14 //
By that word [“tat”], there is a reflective reference to the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.
"Paryāya" (succession) is the absence of simultaneity;
for this very reason, there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here.

And this [type of simile] is twofold: in the case of the commonality of attributes (*dharmasādhāraṇya*) and in the case of the description of the object and its counterpart (*vastuprativastunirdeśa*).
Regarding the first, as for example:
"The water is like the sky, and the sky is like the water; the swan is like the moon, and the moon is like the swan."
The stars have the appearance of water-lilies, and the water-lilies have the appearance of stars.
In the second type, for example:
"Where the ponds, possessing lotus-faces with beautiful reflections, appear like women; and the women, possessing faces as beautiful as lotuses with their own reflections, appear like ponds."
START Sūtra 15:
Memory is the recollection of another object resulting from a similar experience. (RuAss 15)
Another entity that is merely similar [to the subject] does not constitute an inference, because there is no invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). For example—
Beholding this child, whose splendor surpasses that of the gods and asuras and who possesses a form exactly like his father's,
I remember the joy of the Raghus wielding his bow for the destruction of those who opposed the sacrifice of Kuśika’s son.
Without similarity, however, there is no memory, and this is not an ornament (*alaṅkāra*). As it is said:
"Here, having returned from the hunt along the Godāvarī, his fatigue dispelled by the breeze from the waves..."
I remember you, my son, as you sat upon my lap in secret within the reed-huts, your head resting there.
And here, regarding the qualifiers of the agent, it is incorrect for them to exist in the state of being remembered rather than in the state of the rememberer.
For the figure of speech *preyas*, however, the object is a memory evoked by a cause other than similarity,
as for example:
"Ah, even in anger, her face is lovely.
Even in this case, because the factors such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) are already suggested, it is not something conveyed by its own word alone; for example, in "atrānugādam" and so forth.
"Those who once beheld you in battle— your forehead struck by a falling spear, the front of the field turned crimson by the gushing flow of abundant blood as you felled your enemies—
their curiosity has now vanished before the fire of Smara, blazing with the mass of flames from the fire of their eyes, which have flared up to burn the unbearable body of Kāma."
In such cases, when there is the experience of another similar object, the figure of speech is *viśeṣālaṅkāra* (the figure of distinction), characterized by the production of an impossible object;
for this is possible even when the cause is shown to consist of a general action.
According to another school of thought, however, this is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic reason).
Thus, these figures of speech have been determined on the basis of similarity, through the equality of difference and non-difference.
Sūtra 16:
When there is superimposition (āropa) with non-difference as the predominant factor, and the object of superimposition is not denied, it is Metaphor (rūpaka).
Because non-difference is primary, there is the actual existence of difference. Superimposition (āropa) is the imposition of one thing upon another;
since it is occupied by both the object and the subject, when the object is denied, it is Apahnuti (concealment).
Otherwise, however, it is *rūpaka* (metaphor) because the subject (*viṣayin*) effects the form of the object (*viṣaya*), which possesses that form;
whereas similarity (*sādharmya*) is indeed already included [within that].
As they say:

"Metaphor (rūpaka) is held to be a simile in which the distinction has become intensified. Thus, because of the superimposition (āropa), there is a heightened identification (adhyavasāya) regarding non-difference; subsequently, based on that, the classification of figures of speech is established.
This [metaphor] is of three kinds: without parts (niravayava), with parts (sāvayava), and transferred (paramparita). The first is twofold: simple (kevala) and metaphorical (mālārūpaka).
The second type is of two kinds only: that which has all objects as its subject matter (*samastavastuviṣaya*) and that which is partially manifest (*ekadeśavivartin*).

The third type, being based on the use of punning words (*śliṣṭaśabda*), is twofold; each of these, in turn, being either a simple metaphor (*kevalarūpaka*) or a string of metaphors (*mālārūpaka*), is fourfold.
Thus, there are eight varieties of metaphor (*rūpaka*).
However, other individual varieties such as those expressed through direct statement (*vākyokta*) or those expressed through compounding (*samāsokta*) are possible; these should be sought elsewhere.
For example, in sequence:
"O beautiful one, when a servant has committed an offense, it is only proper for masters to strike him with their feet; therefore, I am not pained."
That your foot is pained by the tips of the thorns of the rising, harsh sprouts of horripilation—surely that very pain is mine.
A fresh handful of nectar for the gods; a sickle for the severing of darkness; a lotus-stalk vine terrified by the face of the *kokila* bird distracted by the celestial Gaṅgā;
a double manifestation of the bow of Love; and a thread of hope for those who have offended their beloveds—the slender form of the moon rises on the first day of the lunar fortnight.

"O King, Kalkī, the ear of the Kali age, I have devoured a vast meal— abundant with heaps of rice as bright as jasmine flowers— served upon the leaf-plate of the expansive sky, and drenched in the thick milk of the buffalo-like waves of the Ganges."
"O Lord of the Earth, this line of the Tamāla forest, thick with your sword, shines like the splendor of the night;
it is here that your youthful valor delights, having forcibly brought the fame of your enemies from the moonlight of the battlefield."
In the phrase "kṣitibhṛtaḥ" (mountains/king), there is a pun (*śliṣṭa*).
This is a case of *paramparita-rūpaka* (metaphorical transference):
"Does it not destroy the luster of the lotus? Does it not bestow delight upon the eyes? Does it not increase the fortune of the fish-bannered god [Kāma] by its mere sight?"
It is true that another cool-rayed moon has risen from your moon-like face; yet, if there were pride in this, such pride surely exists here too in your bimba-fruit lip, which is filled with nectar.

In this instance, there is a metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) of the nectar of the lower lip with the celestial ambrosia (*pīyūṣa*), based on the metaphorical identification of the moon-like face.

"O Swan of the minds of the wise! O Sun that causes the lotuses of the faces of enemies to close! O Blue-Red One (Śiva) to the enemies who are the Durgās (fortresses)! O Fire to the acceptance of fuel (the enemy's troops)!

O Expert in bestowing love for the truth! O Terrible One in the preeminence of victory! O Lord, O Excellent Hero, may you perform the imperial rule of Brahmā for a hundred years! [In this verse, the various epithets metaphorically identify the King with the Swan, the Sun, Śiva, Agni, and Bhīma, respectively.]

In this case, there is first the superimposition "you alone are the *haṃsa* (swan)," followed by the superimposition "the mind itself is the *mānasa* (lake)," and so forth; thus, this is a *śliṣṭa-śabda-mālā-paramparita* (a series of metaphors based on punning words).
"I seek refuge with my mind, speech, and body in the compassionate Lord of the World, the pair of feet of Hara, which is a boat for crossing the ocean of birth, old age, and death."

"The sword of the Indra of Mālava triumphs in battle: it is a couch for the Fortune of Kingship, a wave of the ocean of manly valor, a banner of fierce victory that has shattered the lineages of his enemies, a silken stream of the water of his flowing generosity, a dark blue cloud for the swan of the fame of the Lord of the Murals who was languishing with fear of combat, and a personal attendant to the Earth."
Here, "the chamberlain of the earth" (*kṣmāsauvidalla*) is a case of *paramparita-rūpaka* (metaphorical transference) that is also *ekadeśavivartin* (partially manifest).
Other varieties such as these have also been indicated at least in brief.
This [rūpaka] is also seen by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*).

"Just as she is a desert for the waters of goodness, a wall of heaven for the paintings of virtuous conduct, a dark fourteenth day of the waning moon for the moonlight of virtues, and a stroke of a horse's tail for the quality of straightforwardness—

how great is the skill of those who, in this Kali age, have served even such a lineage of kings, when compared to service rendered to the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva), who is easily accessible through devotion alone?"

And here, although that which is being superimposed possesses the gender and number of its substrate (*dharmin*), there are cases where, even though it cannot inherently possess a connection with number, it takes on the number of the object [of superimposition] because the superimposition occurs distributively.
For example: "In some places, the cheeks of the sage—wearing matted hair and bark garments—are like forest fires," and so forth.
For there is no plurality in the sage Kapila.

The poison born from the serpent-cloud forcibly brings about dizziness, distress, mental exhaustion, dissolution, fainting, darkness, physical prostration, and even death for women separated from their lovers.
In this instance, there is indeed *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in the word *viṣa*, which is governed by the meaning of "poison" and brought forth by a specific effect with a fixed number [of meanings].

Since the phrase *jaladabhujagajam* (born from the cloud-serpent) serves as the establisher of the *rūpaka* (metaphor), and because that [metaphor] was not previously established, they say that the word *viṣa* is not a case of *śliṣṭa-śabda-paramparita-rūpaka*; rather, there is only *śleṣa* here. Thus they say.
(Sūtra 17)
When that which is being superimposed is useful for the subject at hand, it is *pariṇāma*.

In *rūpaka* (metaphor), that which is superimposed lacks utility for the subject at hand; therefore, it relates to the subject solely by way of coloring it. In *pariṇāma* (transformation), however, there is utility for the superimposed object precisely because it takes on the nature of the subject;
thus, the subject transforms into the form of the superimposed object.
Because there is no manifestation of coming, following, or departing, this differs from the Sāṃkhya concept of transformation (*pariṇāma*).
That [metaphor] is of two kinds due to its employment in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
The first is as follows:

"Having crossed the celestial river that forms a garland upon the head of the Lord of Beings, he, being the third [person], offered to the boatman—who was actually Lakṣmaṇa—the fare consisting of his friendship."
Followed with difficulty by Śabara maidens whose breasts were as large as a fathom’s span, their eyes raised up in curiosity, he departed quickly for that mountain Citrakūṭa.
Here, the friendship with the son of Sumitrā (Lakṣmaṇa), which is the subject at hand, is transformed into the nature of another form—the boat—by being superimposed as having a common substratum.
This is because the boat is utilized in the context [of the verse] by way of its being the form of friendship.

Thus, here, just as in *samāsokti* (speech of concise expression), that which is superimposed is useful for the subject at hand, and it remains there by virtue of being the very self of the object of superimposition.

For this very reason, there is a superimposition of that conventional usage upon it; it should be understood in the same way here as well, with only this difference: in that case, only the object (*viṣaya*) is explicitly employed, because the subject (*viṣayin*) is already implied.
In this case, however, both are explicitly mentioned; yet, because of their identity, both possess the quality of transformation.
An example of the second type is as follows:

Then, first he paid his respects to the lord of the earth with eloquent words that were refined, full of flavor, and composed in a circuitous style; only thereafter did he present the horse and other gifts.
In the case of a royal assembly, however, a gift is appropriate;
and since that [gift] here takes the form of speech, there is a transformation of words into the nature of a gift through their being placed in a different grammatical relation (vyadhikaraṇa).
START Sūtra 18:
When the object is being doubted, there is doubt.

When non-difference is predominant, there is simply a superimposition (āropa). The subject under discussion is the contextual object, upon which the non-contextual object is superimposed and thus becomes the basis for doubt.
When there is doubt regarding the non-contextual (aprakṛta), the object itself is indeed doubted.

Therefore, when a doubt is raised by the poet's imagination (*kavipratibhā*) as pertaining to both the contextual (*prakṛta*) and the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), it constitutes the figure of speech *saṃdehālaṃkāra*.
And that is of three kinds.
It is pure, contains certainty within it, and concludes with certainty.
It is "pure" when the very doubt reaches its final resolution,
as for example:
"Is she a fresh sprout bursting forth from the abundance of sap of the tree of youth? Or is she a wave surging from the play of the ocean of loveliness?
Or perhaps she is the very staff of instruction for the God of Love himself, who, filled with intense longing, confidently imparts his teachings at the proper time?"
That which begins with doubt, has certainty in its middle, and ends with doubt, has certainty as its core.
For example:
"Is this the sun? But that [sun] indeed moves with seven horses. Is it fire? But that does not certainly spread through all directions."
Having gazed at you for a long time in battle, your adversaries harbor doubts, wondering: "Is this Kṛtānta himself, the one whose vehicle is the buffalo?"

*Niścayānta* (conclusion with certainty) is where there is doubt at the outset and a resolution in the conclusion. For example: "Is it the moon? Where is the spot? Is this a lotus? Where has the water gone?"
"O deer-eyed one, by means of her playful and charming words, it is certain that this face is [the moon] and nothing else."
Sometimes, that which is being superimposed is seen as having different substrata, as for example:
"Are the various trees and mountains colored [by twilight], or has the sky been bent down? Or have they been scattered?"
Has the earth been filled with unevenness, or have the quarters of the sky been withdrawn by the darkness?
In this context, regarding the object of superimposition (*āropa*), the darkness (*timira*) is superimposed upon passion (*rāga*) and so forth as having a locus distinct from trees and the like.
Some, however, state that this is a form of doubt (*saṃdeha*) based on the locus of determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Others, on the other hand, because the particle *nu* indicates probability (*saṃbhāvanā*), describe this as a form of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
START Sūtra 19:
The cognition of another object due to similarity is error. RuAss_19 //
Because it shares the common characteristic of being non-correct knowledge (*asamyagjñāna*), its definition follows immediately after that of doubt.
Error (*bhrānti*) is a property of the mind;
that mode of expression in which this [error] exists is "erroneous" (*bhrāntimān*).
And the object of this [superimposition] is an error induced by similarity, as for example:
"With the expectation that her lips were bimba-fruits, with the thought that her curls were ripe jambu-fruits, and with the delusion that her red cheeks were pomegranate fruits..."

O King, by its very completion, it instantly caused those whose eyes were like lotus petals to become exhausted in the desert; even the parrots in the cages of the Gurjara king fainted from thirst immediately.
However, confusion caused by a severe blow to a vital organ (*marmaprahāra*) and the like is not the province of this figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*).
For example:
"By him whose entire chest was pulverized by the blow of Dāmodara..."
And the wrestler Cāṇūra beheld the sky filled with a hundred moons.
Even an error caused by similarity is accepted only when it is evoked by the poet's creative intuition for the sake of artistic embellishment,
as in the examples cited;
it is not accepted when it arises spontaneously, as in the case of mother-of-pearl being mistaken for silver.

In the same way, it should be understood that even in a doubt such as "it might be a post or it might be a person," there is a conceptual representation (*ullekha*) consisting of the apprehension of a single object in multiple ways due to the influence of various causes.
Where a single object is perceived in multiple ways, that is *ullekha* (multiplicity of description), because it involves the delineation of a plurality of forms.
And this is not a mere *ullekha* without a cause;
rather, it is produced by virtue of the cause known as the possession of various attributes (*nānāvidhadharmayogitva*).
In this regard, inclination, desire, and proficiency are the respective motivating factors.
As it has been said:
"It differs according to inclination, according to desire, and according to proficiency."
Even the appearance [of an object] is a single entity when established through synthesis.
Thus [it is said].

For example, in the *Harṣacarita*, during the description of the district named Śrīkaṇṭha, it is said: "It is a grove of asceticism by the sages, a seat of love by the courtesans, and a hall of music by the dancers," and so forth.
Here, indeed, the single district named Śrīkaṇṭha is described as having many forms—such as a grove of asceticism and the like—due to its association with those respective qualities.
Furthermore, the factors of aesthetic appeal (*ruci*), intention (*arthatva*), and linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) can generally be applied both collectively and individually.

Now, one might object: "In such instances as *'avajravañjaram'* [used by those who have sought refuge] or *'asuravivaram'* [used by the Vātikas], there is the employment of the figure of speech called metaphor (*rūpaka*); how then can this be the province of the figure of speech called *ullekha*?
True.
First of all, there exists a domain for this [figure] distinct from metaphor (rūpaka), such as in the example "the penance-grove" (*tapovana*),
where the actual identity with that [object] is possible.
However, where a metaphor is established, if this mode [of comparison] is also possible there, let there be a commingling (*saṃkara*) of the two.
However, its non-existence cannot be asserted on this basis alone;
consequently, there is no fault whatsoever.

For in that case, let it be the figure of speech *bhrāntimad* (the presence of error), since it is based on the perception of something that does not possess a certain nature as possessing that nature.
This is not so;
for there is no such unprecedented excellence known as "perception in various ways," and this ornament is caused by that very excellence.
If you admit that the perception of confusion is indeed accepted, then let there be the poetic figure *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of "difference within non-difference.
This is not a fault.

The conclusion is that because it is delineated through multiple *dhātus* by means of the differentiation of objects known as the difference among perceivers—and because that [differentiation] takes the form of a distinct interruption—it is in no way possible to include it [within the other figures].
For example: "By the elderly women he was perceived as ‘Nārāyaṇa,’ by the young women as ‘Śrīvallabha,’ and by the children, out of curiosity, he was likewise seen as such."
"He is called Nārāyaṇa by those of advanced age, Śrīvallabha by young women,
and by children, moreover, he is thus confirmed out of mere curiosity. In this same way,
[the meaning] is to be understood in such cases as "Pṛthu in speech, Arjuna in the chest," and so forth.
However, this is the distinction: in the former case, there was the delineation of multiple meanings through a difference in perceivers, whereas here it is through a difference in objects.

But one might object: since the delineation of multiple meanings occurs here by way of the forms of the teacher and so forth, this is *śleṣa* (paronomasia); why then is it established as a separate figure of speech?
True;

however, since another interruption (*vicchitti*) is observed here due to the various elements and signs (*anekadhātvanimitta*), *śleṣa* (paronomasia) would be the cause for the arising of that impression.
But it is not the case that it is entirely absent.

Therefore, this is a distinct figure of speech (alaṅkāra), because even in the absence of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) in such a context, there exists a specific charm (*vicchitti*). Consequently, in cases such as these, *ullekha* alone is superior. Likewise, this figure of speech should be illustrated by relying on the charm of other figures of speech as well.
START Sūtra 21:
Apahnuti (Concealment) occurs when there is a denial of the object [of comparison]. // RuAss_21 //
This is stated by way of contrast with the denial (*apahnava*) introduced [previously], namely that there is the cognition of another object.

Since this occurs in the context of superimposition (*āropa*), when there is a denial of the locus of superimposition while there is cognition of that which is being superimposed, it is the figure of speech called *apahnuti*. And its formal manifestation (*bandhacchāyā*) is threefold.
There is superimposition preceded by concealment, and concealment preceded by superimposition.
Concealment is indicated by words such as "quibble" (chala) and others that establish unreality.
In the first two types of division mentioned above, there is a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*);
in the third type, however, there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*). An example of the first is as follows:
"That which displays the grace of a water-lily within the moon, the world calls a hare; it is not so for me.
I, however, consider the moon to be one whose body is marked by the scar of a wound from the falling meteor-like side-glances of young women overcome by separation from their lovers."

When the hare of the moon is denied (i.e., when the moon is treated as if it were not the moon), the superimposition (āropa) of the moon—which possesses a scar-like mark resembling a rabbit—does not sustain the logical connection (*anvaya-ghaṭanā*); thus, [the previous example] is not faultless. However, that [following example] is as follows: "This orb, radiant with its expansive luster and possessing a body of exquisite beauty, does not rise toward the expanse of the sky like the full moon. Rather, it is now the raised parasol of the burden-bearing [Earth], who is intent solely on the task of shattering the pride of people swollen with vanity through the splendor of her pale [ash-colored] garments. In this case, the superimposition of the moon upon the orb is not intended; rather, the orb is identified as the parasol of the Earth. Therefore, since the superimposition is not the primary focus, there is no lack of logical consistency. Thus, this is considered a faultless instance of *apahnuti*.

The second example is as follows: "May that Kumāra grant you the glory of celibacy— he who always dwells upon the peaks of Mount Saṃyama, which are like groves of blue lotuses to the eyes of the shimmering celestial nymphs, but who does not abide upon the peacock, despite its beautiful plumage."
The third example is as follows:
"By the guise of the pearls scattering from the pure strings of necklaces swinging on the high breasts of Gūrjara women— breasts agitated by trembling as they fled their houses in panic—
the moon, the king of beasts, has fallen along with your enemies as they flee into the empty desert at the pursuit of your fame."
With drops of perspiration as large as jasmine buds.
In this context, it will be established that when the word *manye* is used in place of the word *śūnya*, there is a "poetic fancy with concealment" (*sāpahnavotprekṣā*).
Furthermore, it will be stated that when the word *manye* is used in a different sentence, such as "I consider [you] to be the moon," there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

Even in this case, although there are two varieties based on the reversal of the sequence of application regarding concealment and superimposition (*āropa*), they are not counted as distinct types because, unlike the previous cases, they do not produce the same strikingness (*citratā*).
In that regard, an example of superimposition preceded by concealment has been cited immediately above.
However, as for concealment preceded by superimposition, it is as follows:
"This female Kāpālika wanders here, white with the smearing of moonlight-ashes, bearing the stars as her bones, and delighting in the passion for the practice of disappearance."
She wanders from island to island, carrying within her the fragrance of the *siddhāñjana* salve applied to the moon’s drinking-vessel in the guise of its spot.
Furthermore, there are instances where unreality (*asatyatva*) is expressed through the form of words denoting another entity, such as "body" (*vapus*); for example:
"In that lake of the nectar of beauty belonging to the deer-eyed one, Smara—surely consumed by Śiva—has surely fallen upon her broad hips.
That this line of smoke, indicating the extinction of the embers of his limbs, transforms into the form of a line of hair within the hollow of her navel."
Thus,
having defined the figures of speech based on superimposition (*āropa*) when non-difference is predominant, [the author] now defines those based on identification (*adhyavasāya*): therein—
When there is a predominance of the operation in the process of determination, it is poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Adhyavasāya is the apprehension of the subject as non-different from the object through the swallowing up of the object;
it is of two kinds: the probandum (sādhya) and the established (siddha).
The probandum is that wherein there is an apprehension of the subject as unreal.

And the unreality (*asatyatva*) of a property residing in the possessor [of that property] (*viṣayin*) when it is superimposed upon the object (*viṣaya*) is due to its being perceived as possible in the possessor but impossible in the object. A "property" (*dharma*) consists of qualities (*guṇa*) or actions (*kriyā*). When there is a perception of the possibility or impossibility of such a property, the unreality of the locus of possibility is perceived therein as being non-ultimate (*aparamārthatayā*), whereas the reality of the other [locus] is perceived as ultimate (*paramārthatayā*).
When something is unreal,
the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its reality upon its perception is what is to be established (*sādhya*);
therefore, the predominance lies in the cognitive operation (*vyāpāra*).
Wherein there is the perception of reality even for that which is in fact unreal for the subject,
and wherein there is existence because of the absence of the previous cause of unreality;
therefore, the primary status belongs to the determined [object].

In that context, when there is a cognition of something as being the object of proof (sādhya), and the emphasis is on the operation [of the mind], it is expressed by such terms as *adhyavasāya* (ascertainment), *saṃbhāvanā* (possibility), *abhimāna* (conceit), *tarka* (reasoning), *ūha* (inference), and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy).
Thus, *utprekṣā* is the imagining of the subject (*prakṛta*) as being the non-subject (*aprakṛta*) due to its connection with the qualities or actions belonging to the non-subject.
And this [fancy] is indicated as being directly expressed (*vācyā*) by means of words such as *iva*.
Furthermore, when [the meaning] is already being understood, the employment of words such as *iva* (as if) occurs.

And that [suggestion], by virtue of being determinable as genus (*jāti*), action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), or substance (*dravyatā*), is fourfold even when these are not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*).

Although this variety also exists when the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) possesses these divisions, they are not counted here because they do not constitute a distinct aesthetic charm (*vaicitrya*).
Since each [of these] is twofold by way of being characterized by the conceit of existence or non-existence, there are eight varieties.
Furthermore, since each of the eight types of distinctions has the nature of either a quality (*guṇa*) or an action (*kriyā*), there are sixteen distinctions.
And since each of those distinctions is twofold by way of being either adopted or not adopted as a cause (*nimitta*), there are thirty-two sub-varieties.
And within each of these, there are ninety-six varieties, consisting of the imagination (*utprekṣaṇa*) of cause, essential nature, and effect.
This is the scope of expressed imagination (*vācyotprekṣā*).
Even therein, since the imagination of the essential nature of a substance (*dravya*) occurs most frequently, the varieties of the imagination of cause and effect must be subtracted from that total.

Although, from the perspective of enumeration, there are this many varieties of *pratīyamānā* (suggested) [utprekṣā], nevertheless, the non-statement of the cause (*nimitta*) is not possible in that case; thus, this variety belongs to the young [poet].
For when words such as *iva* are not employed and the cause is not mentioned, the act of imagining (*utprekṣaṇa*) lacks a basis for its establishment.
Generally, in cases of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature), there is a designation of difference according to the possibility of the case.

This [fancy] relies upon the meaning; in the domain of *dharma* (quality), it is sometimes caused by a word with double meaning (*śliṣṭaśabda*). Although it may begin as a simile (*upamā*) at the stage of the syntactical connection of the word-meanings through the expression of similarity, it ultimately culminates in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) by means of a process that ascends to the operation of the cognizer, through the force of the intended purport of the sentence-meaning.
In some cases, when words such as *chala* (deceit) and so forth are employed, there occurs *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (poetic fancy involving concealment).

Therefore, due to the variety of the modes already mentioned and those yet to be described, this [figure] is infinite. For now, however, it is illustrated by way of a mere indication of its direction.
Among these, an illustration of *jātyutprekṣā* (genus-based poetic fancy) is as follows:
"May that moon protect you—curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk, which shines placed upon the head of the Enemy of Smara (Śiva), tawny with fire;
appearing like a sprout, white as crystal, emerging from the skull-bowl that is moistened day after day by the flowing waters of the Mandākinī."
Here, because the word "sprout" (*aṅkura*) is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), a genus is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
An example of a fancy involving action (*kriyotprekṣā*) is:
"The darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium."
Here, the actions of smearing and raining are poetically imagined (utprekṣyete) as being the nature of darkness and the sky respectively;
however, in the second half [of the verse], it is said: "Like service to a wicked person, my vision has become fruitless."
In this case, there is only a simile (*upamā*), not a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
An example of the poetic fancy of quality (*guṇotprekṣā*) is as follows:
"This is that very spot where, while searching for you, I dropped a single anklet upon the ground."
It was seen as if observing a vow of silence out of the sorrow of separation from your lotus-feet.
In this case, suffering (*duḥkha*) is the quality (*guṇa*).
An example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on substance (*dravya*) is as follows:
"Having beheld this netherworld (*pātāla*), which is empty of the moon—the delight of the eyes—"
"Here, by means of the guise of their own faces, the women have created, as it were, a creation consisting of moonlight within the sky."
Here, because the moon is a single entity, it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*).
These are examples regarding the conceit of existence (*bhāvābhimāna*).
Regarding the conceit of non-existence (*abhāvābhimāna*), for example:
"Alas, her two cheekbones, having become so emaciated, have reached such a state of endurance that they seem unable to bear one another, as if they could no longer see each other."
In this case, the phrase "not seeing" involves the misconception of the non-existence of the action.
The same should be understood for [the non-perception of] genus and so forth.
As for the quality being the cause [of cognition], it is as follows:
In the example cited as "curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk," [the cause] is that of curvature.
As for an action, it is as in "having reached such a state of emaciation," where [the cause] is the reaching of emaciation.
These are examples of the employment of a cause (*nimittopādāna*).
An example [of the latter] is: "In the absence of grasping, darkness, as it were, smears the limbs," and so forth.
An example of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause) is: "As if out of the pain of separation, it has become silent," and so forth.
An example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) is: "When the sun, transgressing the proper season, set out to travel toward the quarter frequented by Kubera..."
The southern quarter exhaled the wind from her mouth like a sigh of resentment.

An example of *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result) is as follows: "The forest edges, thorny with brambles, tore open the forehead-skin of the Cola king who had fled in fear—as if to read the letters [of his fate], wondering: 'What indeed will he experience even today?'"
Thus, the direction for examples of expressed *utprekṣā* has been given.
An example of implied (*pratīyamānā*) *utprekṣā* is as follows:
"O fortunate one, she, unable to endure [your absence], dwells within your heart which is filled with other women."
Day after day, with no other occupation, she makes her already slender body even more emaciated.
"O fortunate one, she, finding no room in your heart already filled with thousands of women,
day after day, with no other occupation, makes even her slender limbs thinner."
In this case,
"not ceasing" (amāantī) is imagined as if it were actually occurring, by virtue of being the cause for attenuation;
the same should be understood regarding other varieties as well.

An example of a cause based on a pun (*śliṣṭaśabdahetu*) is as follows: "He who was celebrated on the surface of the earth as a singer of songs established through his peerless uniqueness, became the ultimate ground for the arrows of Love that arrived in a frantic rush of 'I-first' competition."
In this context, regarding the subject of *dharma*, the word *mārgaṇa* (seeker) is used with double meaning (*śliṣṭa*).

An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) beginning with a simile (*upamā*) is as follows: "May those streaks of dark hue on the neck of Śrīkaṇṭha [Śiva]—which act as musk-paste tilakas upon the tablet of the Goddess’s forehead, which act as bees upon her lotus-face, which act as ornaments of fresh tamāla buds upon her head, which act as blooming blue lotuses upon her ears, and which act as applications of black aloe-wood paste upon the slope of her breasts—spread auspiciousness for you."

In this regard, although at first glance there is the perception of a simile (*upamā*) due to the rule "the suffix *kvip* is added after all nominal stems" when *kvip* is prescribed following a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), nevertheless, because the possibility of a standard of comparison is appropriate in the present context, it culminates in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), which arises from the suggestion of a probability.
This is as, for example, in the description of separation: "The armlets acted as bracelets," and so forth.
This [type of simile] has also been illustrated by me in the *Harṣacarita*, in the *Sāhityamīmāṃsā* regarding the scope of the *samastopamā* and *pratīpa* figures, and in various other sections;
however, it is not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length.
An example of *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (a poetic fancy involving concealment) is as follows:

When the city’s playful women hurriedly reached the bank after being struck by a timingila fish, the Siprā river there appeared as if laughing with loud bursts of pearls under the guise of its shimmering mass of foam.
In this case, by the power of the word *eva* (only/just), a possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) is understood, and by the use of the word *chala* (deceit), a concealment (*apahnava*) is understood.
The same should be understood when words such as *chadman* (guise) and others are employed.
In expressions such as "another Indra," if the word *apara* (another) were not used, this would be a mere simile (*upamā*).

However, when that [word *iva*] is employed, since there arises a possibility of identification (*adhyavasāya*) based on the perception of the subject at hand—the king—as Indra (*pākaśāsana*), and since its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is perceived through the word *iva*, this is indeed a case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).

When the word *iva* and others are not employed, because the identification is established as a fact (*siddhatva*), it is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). But when both the words *iva* and others are absent, it is metaphor (*rūpaka*).

Thus, within such a variety of forms of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), in the case of *hetūtprekṣā* (fancy regarding cause), that attribute (*dharma*) belonging to the subject which one fancies as the cause is, by virtue of the process of identification (*adhyavasāya*), treated as non-different from it and adopted as the basis (*nimitta*) for the fancy;
and that [attribute] necessarily exists only as the expressed (*vācya*).
Otherwise, with respect to what would there be a cause?
As in the verse beginning "As if not seeing each other," and so forth;
here, the non-seeing is imagined as the cause for the emaciation that has been presented as belonging to the two cheeks, which are the subjects under discussion (*prakṛta*).
The cause-and-effect relationship and the attainment of a state of frailty constitute the basis (*nimitta*) therein.

Thus, in the verse "It appeared as if bound in silence due to the sorrow of separation from your lotus-feet," the cause for the silence residing in the anklet is its state of being pained. When that [silence] is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*), it should be understood that silence itself is the basis.
The same applies everywhere.

In the case of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature), where a subject (*dharmin*) is fancied as being contained within another subject, the quality (*dharma*) serving as the basis for that fancy is sometimes specified,
as in the verse beginning "May he protect you with his drum" (*sa vaḥ pāyādunduḥ*).
In this context, qualities such as crookedness (*kuṭulatva*) are indeed explicitly mentioned;
however, in instances such as "the shore of the ocean of passion," qualities such as being a cause of agitation (*saṃkṣobhakāritva*) are understood through implication.
Furthermore, where a quality itself is imagined as residing in the subject (*dharmigata*), there too [the figure is divided] based on whether the cause (*nimitta*) is explicitly stated or not.
Regarding the *upādāna* (appropriation), as it is said:
"When he was established in this [state] after attaining consecration,
the earth— its knowledge being obliterated— trembled as if overwhelmed by fear."
In this case, regarding the poetic fancy (utprekṣā) that [the darkness] is overwhelmed by fear because it has reached the ground, the cause such as trembling is explicitly stated.
As for the case where it is not stated, consider examples such as "The darkness, as if smeared, covers my limbs.
Here, in the poetic fancy that the darkness acts as the agent of the action of smearing because it pervades [the body], the cause such as spreading is understood through implication.
In cases such as malice (*vyāpāda*), however, another cause would have to be sought for the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*);
moreover, it is not logical for the object itself to be merely implied (*gamyamāna*),
because it is more appropriate to express that which is already under discussion (*prastuta*) as the basis (*ādhāra*) of the fancy.
Therefore, what has been stated is indeed correct.
In the case of a *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding a result), that which is its cause is precisely its *nimitta* (the ground for the fancy).
If that [cause] were not taken up [as the subject], of what could it be said to be the result?
Therefore, in that case, there is only the apprehension of that sign (nimitta) and no other mode;
as it is said:
"for the turning back of those staying in the chariot, like [the unyoking] of old vehicles."
The sun set out toward the northern direction, the land of birth for those who have transcended the realm of horses.
In this instance, going toward the northern direction is presented as the very cause and occasion for the result of turning the horse.

Although these various stages of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) exist in great abundance within the objects of literary expression (*lakṣya*), they have not been elaborated upon here because they are difficult to discern;
furthermore, just like words such as *iva*, the word *manye* is also an indicator of that [fancy].
However, I believe that when the full conditions for *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) are absent, the use of the word *manye* (I think) expresses only *vitarka* (speculation),
as was previously illustrated in the example beginning: "I think the moon is the separation from you caused by your enemies," and so forth.

Having thus determined that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) occurs when the process of identification (*adhyavasāya*) is the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*), he defines *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) as occurring when the identified [object] is predominant:
"But when the identified [object] is predominant, it is *atiśayokti*. (RuAss 23)
In the process of determination (*adhyavasāna*), three factors are possible: the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the object (*viṣaya*), and the subject (*viṣayin*).
For when the object is swallowed up within by the subject, the essential nature of the determination arises.
In that regard, when [the determination] is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the essential nature is primary.

When [the object] is established as accomplished (*siddhatva*), however, there is the predominance of what has been determined (*adhyavasita*). The predominance of the objective referent (*viṣaya*) is simply not possible within the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*). And when there is the predominance of what has been determined, that is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
And there are five other types:
non-difference within difference,
and difference within non-difference.
There is non-connection where there is connection,
and connection where there is no connection;
and there is the destruction of the temporal sequence between cause and effect.
In that regard, non-difference within difference is as follows:
"The lotus is not in water, and the two blue lotuses are in the lotus; these are upon a golden creeper, and she herself is delicate and beautiful—what is this succession of marvels?"
Here, there is non-difference between the face and so forth and the lotus and so forth, despite their difference.
An example of difference within non-difference:
"Her loveliness is unique; her manner of speech is also some indescribable grace.
That woman is simply the ornament of the Lord of Love himself."

"O Lord of Beings, there exists another beauty and some other kind of grace of conduct; yet a dark-complexioned woman like her could not have been produced even by a mere stroke of the Creator's brush."

In this case, although qualities such as *laḍahatva* (gracefulness) and so forth are non-different [from the object], they appear as different through their distinctness. Or, for example: "When the same beloved's mouth has been obtained by chance, forcibly kissed, and approached by her own will, the various differences in flavor are experienced one after another."
"Even upon the single lip of a beloved— one obtained on the road, one received by force, and one offered of one's own accord— there arise different varieties of aesthetic flavor."
Here, although the taste of the beloved’s lip is non-different [from the speaker], it is presented as distinct through a division of objects.
An example of "non-connection where there is connection" (*asaṃbandhe asaṃbandhaḥ*) is as follows:
"No expense of the wealth of beauty was reckoned; great suffering was voluntarily endured; a fever of anxiety was produced in the heart of people wandering at will."
This poor girl too is ruined by the absence of a lover worthy of her own virtues; what purpose was placed in the Creator's mind when he fashioned her slender form?

Here, although there is a connection with the expenditure of the wealth of loveliness (*lāvaṇya*), a lack of connection (*asaṃbandha*) is established for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of the slender maiden’s loveliness. Or, for example: "In the creation of this [maiden], was the Moon the Creator, the bestower of radiance? Or was it Love himself, whose sole essence is passion? Or was it the month, the source of flowers?
How else could the ancient Sage, dulled by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from sensual objects, have been able to fashion such a captivating form?"
In this instance, although there is a connection regarding the creation by the ancient Prajāpati, a lack of connection is expressed.
An example of a connection where there is no connection is as follows:
"If a flower were placed upon a sprout, or a pearl were set within a bright coral..."
Then he should imitate that clear smile of hers, whose radiance spread across her copper-colored lips.

In this case, there is a connection based on possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), as for example: "Burning is quenched by a stream of water; the rising steam has been observed by her glance; her sighs cause the flickering flames of the lamps to tremble; her body is submerged in pallor.
What more shall I say? Her condition remains such that she stays all night long with her hand held over her face like a parasol to ward off the moonlight from the breeze blowing along your path."
In this case, although there is no actual connection between burning and the spreading of water from a lamp and so forth, a connection is stated as if it were established.
This constitutes a subversion of the temporal sequence of cause and effect, either through a reversal of that sequence or through simultaneity.
An example of such a reversal is as follows:
"O beloved of women, her heart was first struck by the arrow of the flower-bowed god;
only later did it come within the range of your eyes."
An example of simultaneity (*tulyakālatva*) is as follows:
"With clouds gathering densely and moving restlessly, and forest breezes fragrant with *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, and *nīpa* flowers—alas, this season has arrived; the wives of travelers have been lost."
Among these five varieties, the statement of non-difference (*abheda*) and so forth regarding difference (*bheda*) has as its domain that which transcends the world.

Therefore, in this case, there is a determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) with respect to that which is called the "excellence" (*atiśaya*), which is the result and the cause by virtue of being the motivator (*prayojaka*).

For instance, in such cases as "The lotus is not in water," although there is a factual difference between the face and the lotus, their actual beauty is determined to be non-different from the beauty bestowed by the poet; thus, even in the presence of difference, [non-difference is perceived].
This is the basis for the statement regarding difference;
and since the identification (adhyavasāya) is established therein, the emphasis is placed on that which is identified.
However, one should not apply the identification of non-difference between speech and the like with lotuses and the like.
Because [the definition] does not apply to cases such as "difference within non-difference" (*abhede bheda*) and so forth;
for in such instances as "another kind of loveliness" (*aṇṇaṃ laḍahattaṇaaṃ*), an excellence of loveliness is identified (*adhyavasita*) with a difference that serves as its cause.
The same should be understood in other cases as well.
It is precisely with this intention that [the other types] are determined to be subordinate.

Among the five types [of *pratibhā*], that type which exists as a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) will be defined in detail for the sake of elaboration in the section on the figure of speech based on causality (*kāryakāraṇatāśrayālaṅkāra*).
Having thus explained the two figures of speech based on explicit determination (*adhyavasāya*), the figures of speech based on implied comparison (*gamyamāna-aupamya*) are now stated.

Among those, since they are twofold—pertaining to the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) and pertaining to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)—the two figures of speech pertaining to the meaning of a word are stated in sequence:

When comparison is implied, there is *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing) when there is a connection with a common attribute between subjects that are either relevant (*prastuta*) or irrelevant (*aprastuta*). (RuAss 24)
For in the initial employment [of this figure], the state of being understood arises from what has been presented.
In that regard, *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing) consists of the connection of contextual or non-contextual meanings through the relation of common qualities or actions.
For example:
The days, adorned with various kinds of fresh lotus petals, attained a state of vivid crimson; and the blooming lotuses, by the power of the sun's rays, reached their full maturity.
In this case, because the description of the season has been introduced, and because the days and the lotuses are the subjects under discussion, the action is "attaining growth.
The same applies to a quality (*guṇa*). For example:
"The yogic belt, the mass of matted hair, the bark of the *tāra* tree, and the deer-skin—
since these are appropriate for your limbs, let it be said [what you seek]."
Appropriateness (*ucitatva*) is a poetic quality (*guṇa*).
An example of [the quality] regarding non-contextual elements (*aprākaraṇika*) is as follows:
"The army of your horses, galloping and falling into his mouth—[a mouth] whose body is as tender as the petal of a blue lotus..."
The dust of the defeated Gūrjara king was wiped away by some slender woman and by your sword-blade, while your fame was spread abroad.
In this instance, with respect to the Gūrjara king, since both the heroine and the sword are non-contextual (aprākaraṇika), the action is "cleansing" (mārjana).
An example of a quality (guṇa) is as follows:
"In whose mind does the softness of your limbs not appear to one who beholds them?"
The hardness of the *mālatī* flower, the crescent moon, and the plantain tree!
Harshness is a quality.
Thus, this [harsh speech] has been explained as being of four kinds.

Having established *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) when the relevant (*prastuta*) and irrelevant (*aprastuta*) subjects are treated separately, *dīpaka* (the illuminator) is now described for when they are combined: "But *dīpaka* [occurs] when there are both relevant and irrelevant subjects. (RuAss 25)
The phrase "the understandability of the comparison" and so forth continues [from the previous definition].

Among two subjects—one contextual and one non-contextual—a common attribute mentioned in relation to one of them serves as a "lighter" (dīpaka) by its incidental assistance or illumination of the other; thus, it gives rise to the poetic figure known as *dīpaka*.
In this case, because terms such as *iva* are not employed, the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood through implication.
And that [relation] is indeed real;
whereas in the former case, it is merely intentional— whether the subject matter is purely contextual or purely non-contextual—
because the relationship of comparison and the object of comparison is established by the context itself.
The designation "property of a word-meaning" (*padārthatva*) is used because of its connection with a single action performed by many [words], and because of its propriety;

however, in reality, since it pertains to the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), there are three varieties of this figure—namely *ādidīpaka*, *madhyadīpaka*, and *antadīpaka*—according as the property occurs at the beginning, middle, or end of the sentences.
The examples follow in order: "The sky shines with the sun, poetry with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and youth with passion."
"O Lord of Men, O Lord of the Earth, by you this entire world has been shaken by your son."
The sky is illuminated by the sun; poetry by aesthetic flavor; youth by love; the lord of rivers by nectar; and this world by you, O Mother of Men.
Having purified the quarters of the sky with her wandering, at the end of the day,
the radiance of the sun— copper-red like the hue of a young leaf— and the sage’s cow both set out to go to their respective dwellings.
"The wealth of misers, the crest-jewels of serpents, the manes of lions, and the breasts of noble women— how could these belong to those who are not dead?"
The wealth of the miserly, the crest-jewel of serpents, the manes of lions, the breasts of noble maidens, and the nectar of the immortals— how could these ever be touched?

Thus, the three types of *dīpaka* involving a single action have been determined. Here, just as *dīpaka* occurs when a single action resides in multiple factors (*kārakas*), so too does *dīpaka* occur when a single factor resides in multiple actions. For example:
Whose mind would not be curious to assist the virtuous, to sustain prosperity, to travel through the sky, and to hear the life-story of great souls?
Here, the mind is indicated as being distinguished by curiosity through its agency in various actions such as providing assistance and so forth. However,
the *mālādīpaka* (garland-like lamp) will be defined in another context by means of a shadow [of this figure].
When a commonality residing in the meaning of the sentence is stated separately in two sentences, it is *prativastūpamā* (simile by parallelism).

Since the meaning of a sentence is composed of the meanings of its constituent words, the discussion of figures of speech pertaining to the sentence-meaning follows immediately after those pertaining to the word-meanings.
Among these, when a common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is expressed once through the use of *iva* and so forth, it is a simile (*upamā*).
It is also the same [simile] when that attribute is expressed more than once through the relationship of *vastu-prativastu* (the thing and its counterpart).
When there is a single mention without the employment of "iva" and so forth, it is a simile (*upamā*).

However, when there is a non-single mention through the relation of thing-to-counterpart (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*), there is either the state of pure commonality or the relation of image-and-reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*).
The first type is the *prativastūpamā*.

If the word *vastu* (thing) signifies the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), then similarity (*sāmya*) is the *upamā* (simile) because it adopts an etymological derivation (*anvartha*) for every sentence-meaning; its separate mention by means of a synonym is solely due to poetic convention (*kāvyasamaya*). The *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration) will be discussed by resorting to the second type [of *vastūpamā*].
Thus, based precisely on this reliance upon comparison, there is the *prativastūpamā* (simile by correspondence),
as in:
"Only the *cakora* birds are clever in the act of drinking the moonlight."
"The people of Avanti alone are skillful in the playful arts of love."
In this case, the cleverness resides in the sentence expressing the standard of comparison regarding a common attribute;
however, in the sentence concerning the object of comparison, it is indicated by the word "nipuṇa" (skillful).
This [figure] exists not only through similarity (*sādharmya*) but also through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
Just as in this very same *Uttarasthāna*,
in the reading:
"The women of Avanti are not clever at erotic play," there is an illustration by way of the relationship between an original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).
In the expression "thirst" (taṣṇā), it is not only the standard of comparison and the object of comparison that are referred to;
rather, by the word "that" (tat), the common property is also recalled.
This [type of simile] is likewise twofold, according to similarity and dissimilarity.
The first is as follows:
"The ocean was indeed crossed by the monkey warriors; however, only Mount Mandara—its massive body submerged in the depths of the netherworld—knows its profound depth."
"Many indeed worship speech as a goddess; however, Murāri, that poet who has endured hardships in the house of his preceptor, knows the essence of essences most thoroughly."
