In this context, although a single property called "possessing the suffix -ñca" (*ñcān*) has been specified, the metaphorical identification (*aupamya*) based on that is not what is intended to be expressed.

Rather, the basis for the intended expression exists precisely in the act of crossing the ocean and so forth, through the reflection [of the action] by means of such things as divine speech and worship.
An example of the second type is as follows:
"You have already directed your mind toward pride; what else remains? Thus have our enemies been struck down.
For darkness persists only so long as the sun has not reached the summit of the mountain of sunrise."
In this case, there is a reflection through the contrast (*vaidharmya*) of being slain and so forth with the location and so forth.
*Nidarśanā* (Illustration) is the creation of a reflection, understood through a connection between things, whether by way of possibility or impossibility. (Sūtra 28)
In the context of producing a reflection, its definition is as follows:

in some cases, a real connection between things, being possible, brings about the state of being an original and its reflection through its own inherent capacity; in other cases, however, because a connection with a real object is impossible due to a contradiction with positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the production of a reflection is implied by that very impossibility.
Among these, an example of a connection based on a possible object is:
"He who places the god Sun upon the position of his crest-jewel,
thereby informing householders that hospitality must be shown to the virtuous."
In this context, because the causative suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of performing an action conducive to that [result], a connection with a real entity (*vastu*) is possible.
An example where a connection with a real entity is impossible is as follows:
"May that [bow] of Yama protect you, which, naturally curved, touches the play of the strung bow of Cupid."
The moon, whose two extremities are licked by the rays of the jewels of the great serpent kings entwined in his matted locks.

Here, the contact with the moon—which is a different entity—from the play associated with the bow of Love is impossible; therefore, it conveys a play similar to that [actual] play. Thus, because there is no great distance [between them], this is called "the conception of a reflection" (*pratibimbakalpanā*).

This too is twofold, based on the distinction between functioning upon the meaning of a word (*padārthavṛtti*) and the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthavṛtti*). The functioning upon the meaning of a word has just been illustrated. An example of the functioning upon the meaning of a sentence is as follows:
"This cleansing of the jewels of your toenails with lac-dye is like whitening the moon with an application of sandalwood paste."
Some, however, say that this is the figure of speech *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration), but that is incorrect;
for *dṛṣṭānta* consists in the relationship between an original (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) between two sentence-meanings that are independent [of one another].

Where, however, another sentence-meaning is superposed upon the contextual sentence-meaning through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there it is precisely *nidarśanā* (exemplification) that is appropriate, as it is rooted in the impossibility of a literal connection.
This is not an illustration;
and thus:
"If this body, so difficult to find even in the inner harem, belongs to people dwelling in a hermitage..."
Indeed, by their virtues, the garden creepers have been surpassed by the wild forest creepers.
In this case, one should not conceive of it as a simile (*dṛṣṭānta*),

because according to the stated logic, it does not fall under the category of illustration (*nidarśanā*). Furthermore, while this [figure] was previously explained by earlier authorities as occurring when the function of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is impossible in the object of comparison (*upameya*), in reality, it also occurs when the function of the object of comparison is impossible in the standard of comparison.
Because in both cases there exists a disruption of the connection [between cause and effect].
For example: "That paleness on the surface of the cheeks of women from Gauḍa, which was observed during their separation, was perceived in the pollen within the clusters of the date-palm blossoms."
Here, the surface of the cheek is the subject under discussion;
since the quality of that [cheek], namely its paleness (*pāṇḍiman*), cannot exist in the pollen of date palms, there is a cognition of a comparison (*aupamya*).
And this type [of figure] occurs even by way of a "chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*) arrangement.
For example:
"O bald-headed one, you hold a plum fruit firmly upon the plum;
out of disgust for yourself, those deceived by the deception of the stalk are being led astray."
This [simile] is also seen occurring sometimes even with a string (mālā), as for example:
"A lamentation has been made in the forest; a corpse has been anointed with unguents; a lotus has been planted on dry land; and rain has been poured for a long time upon barren soil."
A dog's tail was bent down, whispered prayers were made into the ears of the deaf, and a mirror was held before the face of the blind—this is what happens when one serves ignorant people.
In some cases, however, it also occurs through the impossibility of a connection with the intended meaning (ākṣipta) implied by the force of a negation (*niṣedha-sāmarthya*). For example:
"When you were enraged, the King of Gurjara did not merely abandon the earth out of fear; rather, he abandoned it along with the deer-eyed women of his court."
With her gait she possesses the grace of a swan, with her face the splendor of the moon, and even with her slender breasts she instantly assumes the charm of the temples of wild elephants.
Here, by the negation expressed through the word *mukta* (released), there is an implication—due to the impossibility of its being otherwise—that the feet have attained a swift gait;

and since that [swift gait] is impossible for those two [feet], it brings about a sense of similarity. Thus, this is an *nidarśanā* (illustrative simile) based on a connection with an impossible thing.
When difference is predominant, *vyatireka* (distinction) occurs when the object of comparison exceeds the standard of comparison, or vice versa. (RuAss 29)
Now follows the exposition of the figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) primarily by way of their differentiation.
Differentiation (*bheda*) means distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*).
And that is twofold.
This occurs because the object of comparison possesses either superior qualities compared to the standard of comparison, or the reverse.
The "reverse" refers to possessing inferior qualities.
The examples follow in order: "Desiring to behold the charming play of your eyelashes with a thousand eyes..."
The swarms of bees do not rejoice in the ponds where the blue lotuses have ceased to bloom.
"It is true that the moon, though waned again and again, waxes ever further;
but cease, be gracious, O beautiful one, for youth once gone does not return."

Here, in comparison with the blossoming blue lotuses, the thousand eyes possess superior qualities due to their being fringed with lashes; and in comparison with the moon, youth possesses inferior qualities,
because [the moon], unlike the hare-marked one, does not return again.
START Sūtra 30:

Sahokti (Conjoint Description) occurs when, between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, one is indicated as predominant while the other is connected with it in the sense of accompaniment. // RuAss_30 //
It is precisely the predominance of distinction [that is meant].
Here, the predominance of distinction is caused by the relationship of primary and subordinate;
and the relationship of primary and subordinate is brought about by the sense of "conjunction" (saha).

In this context, the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is determined by intention (*vaivakṣika*), since both may be either relevant to the context (*prākaraṇika*) or irrelevant (*aprākaraṇika*).
For, by the force of the meaning of the word "together" (*saha*), they possess equal status.
In that context, because that which ends in the third case is necessarily subordinate (*guṇa*), it possesses the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*);
and by implication, because the remainder is predominant (*pradhāna*), it possesses the status of the object of comparison (*upameya*).
Furthermore, in this case, the distinction between the subordinate and the predominant is determined by the word itself.
In reality, however, there may even be a reversal;
in that case, this [figure] is invariably rooted in hyperbole (*atiśayokti*).
And that [hyperbole] takes the form of a reversal of the fixed rule governing cause and effect, as well as the form of an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*).

And the determination of non-difference is based either on *śleṣa* (punning) or otherwise. Furthermore, "conjunction" (*sāhitya*) here should be understood as having various distinctions, such as those of the agent and so forth.
And therein—
The form consisting of the reversal of the fixed rule of cause and effect is as follows:
"Her anguish increases all the more along with your offenses.
Here, although the offenses are the cause of the anguish, they are presented as being simultaneous.
An example of [superimposition] consisting of the identification [of two things] based on the wall of a pun (*śleṣa*) is as follows:
"The sun has set along with his enemies; let the armies be withdrawn.
Here, the act of "setting" (*asta-gamana*) is a pun.
Because the word "astam" has both meanings.
An example of that which is otherwise is as follows:
"Now, the pairs of *cakravāka* birds part company along with the groves of night-lotuses.
Here, the act of parting (*vighaṭana*) is distinct due to the difference in its relata, but it is not based on a pun (*śliṣṭa*).
The mere mention of something together with another, without excluding their specific distinctions, is not a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
For example, in such passages as: "Dwell with him on the shores of the ocean, rustling with groves of palm trees."
These very examples illustrate the conjunction of agents (*kartṛ-sāhitya*).

As for the conjunction of objects (*karma-sāhitya*), it is as follows: "In the battle of the stars (*tārakāmaya*), the celestial host, its desires thwarted, was made by him—along with Death himself—to serve as a slave under the command of his discus."

Here, with respect to the action of "making" (*karoti-kriyā*), both the people of the world and death possess the status of the object (*karman*). And this [status of being an object] is also seen to occur even with the suffix *māsa* (the passive marker).
For example:

That bow of Īśvara was lifted up along with the horripilation of Kauśika; it was bent down together with the faces of the kings; it was drawn back simultaneously with the doubt-filled mind of Janaka; it was suddenly pulled forth along with the heart of Vaidehī; and then it was broken together with the sprout of Bhārgava’s mature arrogance.
START Sūtra 31:
He defines *vinokti*, which is the counterpart to *sahokti*—the figure of speech consisting of simultaneous mention:
"The absence of the existence or non-existence of one thing without another is *vinokti*. (RuAss 31)
The absence of existence (*sattva*) is non-existence (*asattva*);
likewise, the absence of non-existence is existence.
When both of these—existence and non-existence—are predicated of something because of its not being present [in another], that is the two-fold *vinokti*.

And here, although it is precisely the presence or absence of beauty and ugliness that ought to be stated, the expression is made by way of their absence in order to demonstrate that "the exclusion of one thing is occasioned by the exclusion of another. In this way, when others are excluded, the positive injunction itself becomes manifest.
An example of the first kind is as follows:
"What prosperity is there without discipline? What night is there without the moon?
And what is the cleverness of speech when it is devoid of true poetry?"

In this context, even without the word "vinā" (without), the intended meaning of "absence" becomes the cause [of the figure] in some way, just as the intended meaning of "together" occurs in the case of *sahokti* (concomitance).
And thus:
"The birth of the lotus was rendered useless, since she did not behold the orb of the moon."
Even the rising of the moon is indeed fruitless for one who has not seen a lotus flower in full bloom.
In such instances, this is indeed *vinokti* (poetic expression by contrast),
because the sight of the moon is perceived as being without beauty for the birth of the lotus;
and this [figure] produces an excellence of charm through the manner of mutual *vinokti*.
In the case of the example cited:
the second [type] is as follows—
“Without the deer-eyed one, [he who was] bold with the splendor of the flash of his intellect regarding various worldly dealings...”
This prince, whose heart is as beautiful as the moon, was [consoled] by that friend.
Here, the absence of lack of beauty is expressed by way of the introduction of a beautiful object;
this is *vinokti* (poetic expression of absence), which is of two kinds.
START Sūtra 32:
Now, two figures of speech based on the charm of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) are described.
Among them, first, he states *samāsokti* (speech by ellipsis), which relies upon the similarity of qualifiers:
"Samāsokti occurs when the unmentioned subject is understood through the similarity of its qualifiers. (RuAss 32)
In this context, there is a twofold division among the relevant (prastuta) and irrelevant (aprastuta) elements: they may be either expressed (vācyatva) or implied (gamyatva).
Furthermore, their expression is also twofold: either by means of a construction involving paronomasia (śleṣa-nirdeśa-bhaṅgyā) or by separate mention (pṛthag-upādāna).
These two varieties together constitute the domain of the figure of speech known as paronomasia (śleṣālaṅkāra).

However, the state of being suggested (gumyatva) residing in the subject at hand is the domain of Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Praise), whereas that residing in what is not the subject at hand is the domain of Samāsokti (Speech in Brief).
And in that case, the cause [of suggestion] is the similarity of the adjectives;
for if there were similarity even of the substantive (viśeṣya), it would result in Śleṣa (Paronomasia).

For, due to the similarity of the qualifying attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*), the suggested non-contextual element is perceived as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for the contextual element. And this state of being a delimiting factor is the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

However, when there is a superimposition of form (*rūpa-samāropa*), because the contextual subject is characterized by that [non-contextual] form through being delimited, it is indeed a metaphor (*rūpaka*).

And that similarity of qualifiers occurs in three ways—through wordplay (*śliṣṭatā*), through commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), and through being pregnant with a comparison (*aupamyagarbhatva*). Among these, an example of wordplay is as follows: "The moon, with its rising passion, seized the face of the night with its trembling pupils in such a way that she did not even notice her entire garment of darkness slipping away from her before her due to that very passion."
In this instance, the apprehension of the behavior of the hero and heroine occurs through the power of the punned (*śliṣṭa*) adjectives;
for there is the cognition of the night and the moon as being qualified by the property called "heroism" (or "heroic status") without their having abandoned their own essential natures.
An example of [this] by way of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) is as follows: "The slender, charming young woman, with tremulous eyes, smiling like a flower..."
"O fortunate one, it attains full bloom merely by the sight of you."

Here, due to the similarity of qualifiers such as "slender" (*tanvī*) and so forth, there arises the cognition of the behavior of a creeper (*latā*) in the tremulous-eyed woman. In that case, the superimposition (*samāropa*) of the property called "expansion," which belongs exclusively to a creeper, is the cause; otherwise, the specific behavior of a creeper would not be cognized through the mere similarity of qualifiers alone.
And in this context, "expansion" (vikāsa) should be understood as used figuratively;
likewise, it should be understood even when there is a superimposition of the effect.
Furthermore, this *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) is less distinct than the former [type].

An example by way of containing a simile (*aupamyagarbha*) is as follows: "The deer-eyed woman is beautifully attired, with the radiance of her teeth like a cluster of flowers, her hands like lovely sprouts, and her mass of hair like a swarm of bees."

In this case, the compound "dantaprabhāpuṣpāṇīva" (the teeth's luster as if they were flowers) is first formed with an underlying simile (*upamāgarbha*) due to her exquisite beauty; subsequently, by resorting to another compound—namely, "citā dantaprabhāsadṛśaiḥ puṣpaiḥ" (strewn with flowers resembling the luster of her teeth)—the conventional status of a *latā* (creeper) is perceived through the power of the shared adjectives. In the very same verse, if the reading were "parītā hariṇekṣaṇā" (surrounded by deer-eyed women), since there would be neither a prover nor a refuter of either a simile or a metaphor, one might initially apply the figure based on their commingling (*saṃkara*); however, subsequently, as before, the perception of the *latā* arises through the greatness of the other compound.

However, although the quality of having common attributes (*samānaviśeṣaṇatva*) may exist here due to the recourse to another compound by virtue of being a "womb of metaphor" (*rūpakagarbha*), it does not serve as the motivator for *samāsokti*.
This is because the apprehension of the further meaning occurs precisely through the medium of a "metaphor with partial manifestation" (*ekadeśavivartirūpaka*), rendering *samāsokti* redundant.
Furthermore, this principle does not apply to cases of the previously shown commingling (*saṃkara*) of simile (*upamā*).

This is because there is no occurrence of the combination of simile (*upamā*) and confusion (*saṃkara*) when they exist as partial manifestations (*ekadeśavivartin*). Furthermore, that partial manifestation of metaphor (*rūpaka*) occurs in two ways: through punning (*śleṣa*) and without punning (*aśleṣa*). An example of the non-punned variety is as follows:
Having gazed upon the face of the woman going to meet her lover in the night with eyes of lightning, the cloud,
along with the falling showers, cried out most piteously as if saying, "Has this moon been vomited forth?"

Here, in accordance with the act of gazing, the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "with eyes like lightning" serves as the basis for the suggested poetic fancy (*pratīyamānotprekṣā*) that the cloud is a beholding man who has cried out most piteously. An example of a *śleṣa* (pun) serving as the basis [for such a suggestion] is as follows:
"In the place for counting love's [debt], displaying an elaborate array of writing by means of the ink of bees placed upon the broad petals of *vicikila* flowers—"

"By means of its crooked scripts, who indeed among the scribes did Spring not unsettle, making them keep accounts of income and expenditure regarding the lives of those separated from their lovers? (Śrīcaṇḍī 6.70)

For here, in the words *pattralipikā* (the leaf-writer) and *yastha* (the scribe), which contain a double entendre (*śleṣa*), there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) based on the phrase *dvirepha-maṣīlava-* (having bees for ink).
Since the scope of application for this [metaphor] is extensive, one should not conceive of it as *samāsokti* (synecdoche).
Thus, this is one type [of *samāsokti*] produced by punning adjectives.
That [type of simile] produced by common qualifiers is twofold, through the superimposition of a dharma and the superimposition of an action.
That produced by qualifiers containing a hidden comparison is twofold, through the mixture of similes and through compounds.
However, the two varieties based on metaphor (rūpaka) are not its domain.
Thus, there are five types of *samāsokti* (synthetic expression).
This *samāsokti* is first threefold: by the superimposition of a pure effect, by similarity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*), and by being composed of both.
Furthermore, the similarity of qualifiers has been determined to be of five kinds.
In all these cases, the lifeblood is precisely the superimposition of conventional usage;
and that consists in the superimposition of the conventional usage of a worldly object upon a worldly thing,
and the superimposition of the conventional usage of a technical (śāstrīya) object upon a technical thing.
Either the superimposition of the conventional usage of scriptural entities upon worldly ones,
or the superimposition of the conventional usage of worldly entities upon scriptural ones— thus it becomes fourfold.
In this way, *samāsokti* (synecdoche) is of many varieties.

In that regard, by way of superimposing a pure action, as for example: "O King, in the desert land, the khadira tree scratches deeply at the breasts, firmly seizes the hair, and draws upon the lovely face an asymmetrical leaf-pattern; it drags the garment from the rounded hips of your enemies' deer-eyed women as they tremble in terror."

Here, the perception of the *khadira* tree as a forceful lover (*haṭhakāmuka*) arises from the superimposition of pure actions such as drawing leaf-designs; this has been illustrated by means of the similarity of adjectives.
An example of [superimposition] consisting of both [the literal and the figurative] is as follows:
"The locks of hair have been plucked out, the chest torn open, the entire lower lip bitten, pain produced in the ear, and an injury inflicted upon the eyes, which possess the beauty of blue lotuses."
As they travel through the desert with footfalls agitated by extreme haste, what have the sapless thorny trees not done to the wives of your enemies?

In this instance, there is a similarity of qualifiers in the words "sapless" (*nīrasaiḥ*) and "thorny" (*kaṇṭakibhiḥ*). In the phrases "whose locks [of hair] have been shorn off" (*nirlūnānyalakāni*) and so forth, there is the superimposition of an effect.
These are the four types of superimposition of behavior (*vyavahāra*), with examples given in their respective order.
For example:

"What did the youth not do out of intense passion— the fire of his eyes, which embraced the sky, kissed the faces of the quarters, and with the tips of its rays (hands) traced the crescent moon that had obstructed the heavens— having submerged the flower-arrows within?"

And worldly objects, through the distinctions of taste and so forth, possess manifold varieties that one may imagine for oneself: "I believe it is certain that those who, seeing You as having a single form even in all Your manifestations, have applied the designation 'infinite' to You— by them, the case-ending expressing 'otherness' has indeed been elided, and thus Your definition has been established."
In this case, there is the superimposition of a thing well-known in grammar upon a thing established in the scriptures and treatises:

"That which has not reached the limit of the eyes, that which has never been associated with nor touched by another word, that for which no simile has ever been seen, that which has not arrived through the force of meaning, and that which is not nothing at all— the indescribable beauty (*lāvaṇya*) of gazelle-eyed women, devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), triumphs as a marvel to the mind."

Here, in the case of beauty (*lāvaṇya*), which is a worldly object, there is the superimposition of an object well-known from the *Mīmāṃsā* treatises. In this same way, the superimposition of objects well known from the sciences of logic (*tarka*), medicine (*āyurveda*), and astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*) is to be understood.
For example:

As Smara displayed his superiority by employing the charming play of his own side once the cause was established, the unbroken expertise of the cuckoo served to destroy the pride of all the young men who were struck by humiliation.
In this context, there is a superimposition of objects well-known from the science of logic (*tarkaśāstra*).
The word "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship) should be explained here through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as referring to the subject at hand.
"The sun-stone became slow and sweet in its heat, and the darkness displayed a swelling."
In the absence of the Lord of Herbs, the [false] views resorted to the defect born of cataracts.
Here, there is a superimposition of things well-known from Ayurveda:

"As you strike at the temples of rutting elephants, as you perform protective rites during the *vaidhṛta* yoga upon the circle of the earth, and as you always conduct the festival of military expeditions among the Lāṭas;

since you do not abandon your auspicious former disposition and remain ever attended [by good fortune], your glories of victory increase. For what indeed is not an auspicious omen for those who possess merit?"
Herein lies the superimposition of objects well-known in the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*): "O best of teachers,
you who have abandoned the state of having limited movement, who are not to be known even by those whose intentions are ever-expanding and who delight solely in valid inference,
and who possess an unprecedented activity."
"Thus determined by the wise, the multitude of your virtues, O connoisseur, is neither to be expressed nor even indicated."
In this case, there is a superimposition of the subject matter well-known from the treatises of Bharata and others;

for here, the designation of "rasa," such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth, is perceived as being inherent in a collection of qualities (*guṇagaṇagatatva*). This is because rasa is not to be understood through the power of implied meaning (*tātparyaśakti*).
Nor is it the object of inference;
nor is it made expressible by words through the operation of denotation;
nor is it within the scope of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

However, because the internal distinctions of the objects of cognition have dissolved, [the aesthetic state] is free from limitation; it is made the object of a unique operation characterized by manifestation (*vyañjana*); and, by abandoning its status as residing in either the imitated or the imitator, it resides in the connoisseur.
Thus, through words such as "by means of spreading implications" (*prasarpattātparyaiḥ*), it is *rasa* itself that is perceived.
Thus it is understood;
in this same way, other [cases] should also be known.
"Where Paśyantī conceals herself within as if out of shame, and where Madhyamā also falters due to the essence of her desire to emerge through sweet sounds;"
O Lord, how can the speech of those who practice the fickleness of uttering flatteries be considered external when compared to the Goddess's own words during her firm embrace in secret play with You?
In this case, there is a superimposition of worldly linguistic usage upon a thing well-known through scripture.

It has been stated previously that worldly linguistic usage regarding things has many varieties due to the distinctions of taste (*rasa*) and so forth. Among these, regarding the superimposition of a pure effect (*kārya*), the definition established according to earlier treatises—namely, "by means of similarity with a qualifier, relying on the figurative status of the effect as a qualifier"—should be applied in some way or another.
But here—
“The autumn, bearing the rainbow upon her pale cloud-breast, resembling a fresh nail-mark,
and pleasing the spotted moon, increased the heat of the sun even further.”
In this case, there is indeed the perception of the sun and the moon as the hero and heroine;
yet, since there is no equality of attributes (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*) here, how could that [perception] arise? [The answer is:
because of the equality of the attribute "making the spotted moon serene," the autumn is perceived as the heroine, and [the description of the sun] conforms to that.

If it is argued that the status of the two as lovers (nāyaka) is understood through the use of *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning), then how is the qualifying attribute "bearing the rainbow of Indra, which resembles fresh nail-marks" indicated by way of similarity?
Furthermore, a partial metaphor (*ekadeśavivartinī upamā*) has not been mentioned here, by whose power the status of the lovers could be perceived.
How, then, is it excluded here? To this it is said: If the simile that occurs in a single part (*ekadeśavivartinī*) has not been stated for every individual word, by whom has it been prohibited?
For that [simile] is possible here as well, since it arrives by way of the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Now, in this case, the hero is not perceived in his own form as the object of comparison; rather, there is the perception of the sun and moon alone as the heroes, because they function as the heroes here. Therefore, although the status of being the object of comparison (*upamānatva*) resides in the phrase "resembling a fresh nail-mark" by virtue of direct expression (*śruti*), it must, upon consideration of the actual matter, be transferred to the rainbow of Indra (*aindra dhanus*).
Because of the perception that "she bears a nail-mark with the luster of Indra’s bow," the injunction is transferred to the object,
as in the case of "He offers oblation with curd.
Thus, this is indeed *samāsokti* (synecdoche) animated by *upamā* (simile).

Furthermore, in this case, the perception of the lake’s beauties as heroines does not arise through *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning), because there is an absence of similarity in the adjectives (*viśeṣaṇasāmya*).

Therefore, the heroine is perceived here as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), rather than the perception of the heroine being established through the attributes of the lake’s beauties; thus, one must admit that this is indeed a *ekadeśavivartinī upamā* (a simile in which only one part is manifested).
Because no other alternative is possible;
for those by whom [the term] has not been mentioned, it must likewise be added as a supplement.

However, in cases such as "by the mass of hair like a swarm of bees," where there is a simile expressed through a compound (*samāsokti*), and where it is possible to apply the identity of adjectives through another compound, there the figure is produced by adjectives containing a simile within them (*aupamyagarbhaviśeṣaṇaprabhāvitā*).
Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever, as this is indeed *samāsokti* (synecdoche).

Then, when the moon was embraced by autumn, the rainy season departed, its lightning-glances subsided;
for what women's virtue of beauty did not perish, their breasts having been stripped away like clouds?
"What concern for women can there be for a high-minded man who desires to conquer the unconquered?
The sun does not enter its twilight rest until it has traversed the entire world."

Here, because of the concealment [of the literal meaning] and the casting of glances like lightning flashes, the metaphorical treatment (*nāyakavyavahāra*) of the moon and the autumn is perceived; thus, the specific meaning embraced by *samāsokti* (condensed expression) is supported by *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general principle), which relies upon a general sense.
And in this case, the emergence of that general sense occurs through the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

The epithet "possessing glances like calm lightning," which contains a simile within it, is identical here by virtue of its reliance on a different type of compound (*samāsa*). However, in cases such as "asamāptetyādi" (beginning with "not completed"), because the word *strī* denotes merely the general quality of femininity, the general meaning is [transformed] through the figure of speech known as *samāsokti*. This *samāsokti* is evoked by a causal connection (*kāryāpanibandhana*) that implies a specific gender, and through it, the behavior of a hero (*nāyaka*) is superimposed [upon the woman].
The general theme is supported by the specific account of Ravi’s encounter with the twilight:
"Because of the halo formed by the sloughing-off of the coils of the Lord of Serpents as they slipped away due to the force of his pulling,
the Mandākinī quickly coiled around the base of his foot for a long time, as if to soothe the pain from the churning."

Here, by the negation of the snake’s slough, the Mandākinī is superimposed; that which is her actual encircling at the base of the feet is apprehended through a *śleṣamūlātiśayokti* (hyperbole based on paronomasia) as an encircling at the base of the [divine] feet.
That apprehension thus gives rise to a *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), imagining it to be "as if for the sake of allaying the pain of churning.
Even as it is being evoked, this *utprekṣā* internalizes a *samāsokti* (speech of brevity) based on the metaphorical relationship of husband and wife between the ocean and the Mandākinī.
Thus, in the cases of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *samāsokti* (condensed expression), there is a single point in time.

Similarly, in the verse "As if they were nail-marks upon the forest grounds," the treatment of the forest grounds as heroines is rooted precisely in a *samāsokti* that has entered into another *utprekṣā*.
In this manner, this *samāsokti* possesses an infinite variety; one should explore it for oneself along these lines.
START Sūtra 33:
*Parikara* is the use of an epithet with a specific intention. // RuAss_33 //
This [type of poetry] is mentioned here because it involves the variety of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).
The quality of having an intended meaning (*sābhiprāyatva*) in qualifiers consists in their containing a suggested sense (*pratīyamānārtha*).
For this very reason, because its words are clear yet profound, this is not the domain of *dhvani*.
And thus, because the implied portion is directed toward the expressed meaning, the name *parikara* (the "elaboration") is meaningful.
"In the presence of King Duryodhana, whose wealth is his honor and who bears the bow, while the Kuru kinsman looks on and even Karṇa and Śalya witness it—
today I have drunk the warm blood from the chest of that very man who dragged away the hair and garments of the Pāṇḍava women, as he was being torn apart by my sharp claws while still alive."
In this context, in the passage beginning with "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*), there is the quality of clarity and depth of expression (*prasannagambhīrapadatva*) intended to convey irony (*sotprāsa*).
Likewise:
"O son of Aṅga, general, favorite of the king, Karṇa who mocks Droṇa..."
This is to be understood from such passages as: "Now protect this Duḥśāsana from Bhīma.
START Sūtra 34:
When there is equality even of the substantive (viśeṣya), the presence of two [meanings] at the outset constitutes *śleṣa* (paronomasia). // RuAss_34 //
The similarity of mere adjectives has been discussed in the context of *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation).
However, this [present discussion] is stated with reference to the similarity of adjectives joined with the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

In that regard, when there is the composition of words with double meaning (*śliṣṭapada*), whether both subjects are contextual (*prākaraṇika*), both are non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*), or one is contextual and the other non-contextual, it is *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Among these, the first two types occur only when there is similarity between both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), whereas the third type occurs only when there is similarity of the qualifier. However, if there were similarity of the qualified, then—given that the primary meaning is restricted by context, purpose, and so forth—this would become the domain of suggestion (*dhvani*) regarding a secondary meaning. In the first two types, however, both meanings are equally expressed as the literal sense (*vācya*).
For this very reason, it is stated here that "the mention of both" refers to the scope of the third variety;
whereas "even when the qualifier is equal" refers to the scope of the remaining two varieties. Examples in order:

May that Mādhava himself, the destroyer of Andhaka, protect you forever—he by whom the body of Bali was formerly made into a woman by the one who has destroyed the mind-born [Kāma]; he who wears a serpent as a garland and bracelets and who bore the Gaṅgā; and whose praiseworthy name the immortals call "the one who took the moon-marked head."
"The sight of those lotuses, reared in the forest, was like seeing those who have been brought to a state of agitation by hunters with many arrows."
"Though its object has arisen entirely of its own will, it cannot be said to 'give'; even with hundreds of entreaties, it bestows only suffering;
and out of delusion, it suddenly snatches away even life—alas, this perverse Lord is like the god of love!"

In this instance, both Hari and Hara possess contextual relevance (*prākaraṇikatva*). Since the lotuses and the deer serve as points of comparison (*upamāna*), they possess non-contextual relevance (*aprākaraṇikatva*).
Thus, Īśvara and Manobhava possess both contextual and non-contextual relevance.
Thus, because it exists as residing in both word and meaning, it is threefold.
Among these, *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal pun) occurs when there is a difference in words due to distinctions in accents such as the udātta and differences in phonetic effort (*prayatna*),
wherein there is generally a breaking up of the words (*padabhanga*).
Semantic paronomasia (*arthaśleṣa*), however, occurs where there is no difference in accent or other phonetic features;
for this very reason, it does not involve the breaking up of words (*sabhaṅgapadatva*).
By combining both, one has "paronomasia of both" (*ubhayaśleṣa*).
"Just as:
'Bearing their blossoming red petals and possessing stalks joined with water,
the lotuses shone forth, having cast aside all their luster upon other flowers, just like ascetics.'"
In this context, in the phrase "raktacchadatvam" (the state of having red petals), there is semantic punning (*arthaśleṣa*);
in "nāla" (not enough) and so forth, there is verbal punning (*śabdaśleṣa*);
and when both are combined, there is punning of both kinds (*ubhayaśleṣa*).
However, for fear of increasing the bulk of the work, it has not been cited separately.
